description: We are a team brought together by a shared interest in science, technology, and art. At NASA Space Apps Barcelona, our goal is to make Earth science more accessible and engaging by combining visualizations from NASA’s Earth Information Center with sound generated in real time. Through the Earth Information Jukebox challenge, we want to help people explore our changing planet through both sight and sound.
summary: Our project is a visual-to-audio data sonification tool that converts satellite imagery and visual map metrics into real-time musical soundscapes. By assigning different auditory layers (such as lead voices and accompaniment tracks) to distinct visual parameters like activity, shape, warmth, hue variability, and contrast, it allows users to experience complex Earth science data through sound.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Orbit Records turns NASA Earth imagery and video into music. You pick a visualization from the NASA SVS / Earth Information Center gallery (shown as vinyl sleeves) or paste an SVS link. The app loads the image or video and reads it as a score. A reading window sweeps across the picture (left to right, right to left, top to bottom, radial, segmented, or full-frame for video). In each window the app measures:

Where the data sits in the frame

Brightness

Colour and spectrum

Pixel density and contrast

Those measurements become notes, rhythm, dynamics and instrument choices. The piece has five tracks (two visual voices, two accompaniment voices and a bass), 32 bars with 8 readings per bar. It plays in real time with Web Audio synthesis and instrument samples, and loops continuously with no cut at the end. The same image always produces the same piece. The user can mute or solo each track, change the reading mode, see the exact area being “listened to” in a lens view, and export the result as a WAV file.

What benefits does it have?

It lets people hear patterns in Earth data (fires, ocean currents, forest height) instead of only seeing them. This helps people who can’t read charts easily or who prefer listening and gives other dimension in the experience of visualization that kind of data or images.

It needs no installation. It runs in the browser and works on mobile.

It works with any NASA SVS visualization, or in any file you can upload.

It is deterministic, so results can be compared and reproduced.

It makes NASA’s public data more approachable and shareable.

What is the intended impact?

To widen access to NASA Earth science for general audiences, educators and visually impaired users, using sound as a second way in. We want people to notice the shape of change (a fire season, a current, a canopy) and then explore the real dataset. It is an awareness and engagement tool, not a scientific measurement instrument. The mapping from image to sound is an artistic and perceptual choice, and we state that openly.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

Front end: a single HTML/CSS/JavaScript file. It uses Canvas for image analysis and Tone.js with the tonejs-instruments samples for sound.

Back end:

A small Python server (server.py) for local development.

A PHP bridge (api.php + .htaccess) on Hostinger. It resolves SVS pages, proxies NASA media and curates the gallery, so the browser can analyse the pixels despite cross-origin limits.

Data: NASA SVS and the Earth Information Center.

Testing: Playwright with Chrome, plus a mock NASA server and PHP tests.

AI assistance: Claude, used as a coding and mentoring assistant.

Hardware: ordinary laptops and phones, with no special equipment.

How is your project creative?

The main difference between our project and similar web apps is that ours creates music. It goes beyond data sonification by combining image data with smooth transitions and musical principles to shape individual sounds into a coherent melody. We turn data into sound, and sound into music.

Also we take the data as sheet music. It also presents the data as a record collection, with vinyl sleeves and a “turntable” feel. The reading modes change how the same image sounds, so a radial sweep of a globe feels different from a left-to-right pass. The music is generative but reproducible, and the continuous loop makes each visualization feel like a track you can leave playing.

What factors did your team consider?

Honesty: the sonification is interpretive, so it should not claim scientific precision.

Accessibility: it works on mobile, with large touch targets and screen-reader labels for people with visual impairments.

Reliability: a static single file plus a minimal bridge keeps hosting simple, and it only fetches from NASA domains.

Consistency: the same input always gives the same music.

Listening experience: the loop is seamless, and the sound should be pleasant, not noise.

Performance: NASA files can be large, so the app picks a suitable, size-limited version of each file.

Fit with the challenge: turn real NASA Earth data into something people can hear and explore.
